title: Nearest Match From a Start Index
statement:
You get an integer array nums, a value target and an index start. The value target occurs at least once in nums.

Among all indexes i with nums[i] === target, return the smallest distance |i − start|. Return the distance, not the index.

examples.why: start itself holds an 8. Taking the first 8 in the array would give 4.
There are 8s one step to the left and one step to the right. Either gives distance 1.
The only 6 is at index 0, three steps away. The answer is that distance, not the index 0.

hints: Scanning the whole array and taking the minimum |i − start| already works. Can you stop early?
The closest match is reached first if you search outward from start: distance 0, then 1, then 2, …
Step d from 0 upward and check start − d and start + d (when in range). The first d that hits target is the answer.

explain.intuition:
The simplest correct answer looks at every index and keeps the smallest |i − start|. That is O(n), which is fine.

You can do better when matches are near start: search outward, like a ripple. Check distance 0, then both indexes at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. The first hit is guaranteed to be the closest, so you stop there. In the worst case you still visit every index, but on average far fewer.
steps: If start − d ≥ 0 and nums[start − d] === target, return d.
If start + d < n and nums[start + d] === target, return d.
Because target exists, the loop always returns before d exceeds n.
pitfalls: Returning the index of the match instead of its distance from start.
Taking the first or last occurrence of target in the array, which ignores where start is.
Stopping the outward walk when one side runs off the array. The other side may still hold the match.

complexity.time: O(n) worst case, O(d) where d is the answer for the outward walk

solutions.title: Scan every index
solutions.idea: Check every index holding target and keep the smallest distance to start.

solutions.title: Walk outward from start
solutions.idea: Two pointers move away from start one step at a time. The first one to land on target gives the smallest distance.

followups: Many queries ask for different (target, start) pairs on the same array. What would you precompute?
The array is sorted. How fast can a single query be?
